newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: N.Korea corn crop seen failing, famine worsening.
newsitem.headline: N.Korea corn crop seen failing, famine worsening.

text.p: North Korea will be driven deeper into famine as its staple corn crop plunges this year due to drought and pest attacks, an expert on the country's agricultural sector said on Tuesday.

"The North's corn output may fall by up to 50 percent this year because of damage from drought and army worms," said a senior grain analyst who is close to official South Korean thinking on the communist north's economy.

A 50 percent drop in the corn crop, harvested between August and early September, would take production down to around 500,000 tonnes, compared with an estimated 1.0-1.2 million tonnes in 1996, when output was hit by floods.

At least 70 percent of the arable land hit by drought in the North was believed to be sown to corn, and rampant army worm infestation would reduce the crop further, the South Korean analyst said, adding the country was in urgent need of fertiliser to boost yields.
He estimated North Korea's total corn crop area at 600,000-650,000 hectares.

Earlier on Tuesday, Ted Yamamori, president of the Food for the Hungry International, said in Seoul at least five million people in North Korea were suffering in a crisis that is reaching "the level of the notorious Somali and Ethiopia famines".
"It is a disaster in the making," Yamamori said in an interview with Reuters.

Yamamori had visited North Korea between July 22-26 to monitor the distribution of 120 tonnes of wheat flour donated by his group, a Geneva-based private agency which offers food aid and development programmes in cooperation with international relief groups.

North Korea also said on Tuesday that a record heatwave in July had seriously damaged crops and other parts of its hard-hit economy. Officials said about a fifth of the country's arable land was seriously affected by drought.
The state-run Korean Central News Agency (KCNA), in a report seen in Tokyo, said the average noon temperature in July was above 35 degrees Celsius in Pyongyang and other areas.
It said temperatures were three to five degrees higher than usual on average and more than 10 degrees higher in some places.
KCNA quoted Ri Jong-u, director of the Central Forecast Institute of the Hydro-Meteorological Service, as saying the heatwave was unprecedented in 61 years of weather observation.

"The bottoms of reservoirs were visible and thousands of rivers and streams had dried up. This seriously affected the growth of crops and made it impossible to supply industrial water through irrigation networks," the KCNA report said.
The report said North Korea could not expect rain for some time.
But an official in the South Korean Meteorological Office in Seoul forecast rains across the Korean peninsular next week would bring some relief.

He said there was no indication the current drought stemmed from the El Nino weather phenomenon which is believed to be causing unusually dry weather in Australia and Indonesia and a so far patchy monsoon in India this year.

Last week, Pyongyang said this year's heatwave and drought had a "catastrophic" impact on its economy and worsened food shortages following two years of floods that devastated substantial areas of farmland.
North Korean officials have said they need some 800,000 tonnes of grain in emergency aid from foreign countries to ease food shortages until the next rice harvest in October.
Government officials in Seoul said they believed there were pockets of areas in the North where people faced famine, but that the problem was due to poor transport and distribution systems.
"Of course the North has serious problems, but on a national scale it could avoid famine with foreign help," said an official at the National Unification Ministry.
